title: Map the data sources
why_matters: By week three you'll be writing SQL against tables you didn't build. The structure of your data warehouse — what's a source, what's a fact, what's a dimension, what's deprecated — shapes what's easy versus hard to answer. The hour you spend in week one walking the warehouse is the hour you save in week six when a stakeholder asks 'can we get this by channel by week?' and you know exactly which table that lives in.
steps: Find the data warehouse (Snowflake / BigQuery / Postgres / etc.) and the orchestration layer (dbt / Airflow / etc.). Open the schema docs if they exist. If they don't, that's a finding.
List the top 10-15 tables by reference frequency (which tables show up most often in the team's dashboards + ad-hoc queries). Read each one's column list.

Identify the canonical fact tables (transactions / events / signups / etc.) and the canonical dimension tables (users / accounts / products). Note which ones are kept clean and which ones have known issues.
Find the dbt project (or equivalent). Read the model file structure. Identify which models are marketed as 'source of truth' and which are downstream consumption layers.

Ask Marcelo (or whoever owns the data warehouse) one question: 'which table looks easy to use but is actually a trap?'. Most engineers will tell you the truth in week one and never tell you in week six.
success_criteria: By end of week, you can describe the top 10 tables and their relationships in plain English. You know which one tablename Marcelo flagged as the trap. You can write a join between users and events that runs without errors.
reflection_prompt: Of the top tables, which one's name doesn't quite match what it contains — i.e. you'd have expected to find one thing and it actually holds another? Two sentences.
